short_summary: Following election results, the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange plunged and the shekel depreciated against major foreign currencies. Simultaneously, leading economists publicly warned against proposals to rely on cryptocurrency if international banking sanctions are ever imposed.

sources.name: Ynet
sources.title: חג הדמוקרטיה הישראלי לא בא טוב למשקיעים

paragraphs: Israel’s financial sector encountered significant turbulence following the publication of the official election results, reversing the notable gains recorded across domestic markets on the eve of the vote. The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange suffered immediate declines across its primary boards, with benchmark equity gauges reflecting broad investor unease. The TA-90 index plunged by 4.6 percent, while the broader TA-125 dropped 2.4 percent and the premier TA-35 fell 1.8 percent. Market selling was heavily concentrated in key cyclical and credit-sensitive sectors, including commercial banking, insurance, and real estate, highlighting an immediate atmosphere of apprehension regarding the emerging political landscape.

The downward pressure was particularly pronounced in construction and property development shares. The specialized construction index lost 8.7 percent, while the broader real estate index contracted by 6.3 percent. Major financial institutions were similarly battered during the trading session, with both the banking and insurance sector indices sliding by approximately 5 percent. Alongside the equity rout, foreign exchange markets registered a sharp depreciation in the value of the Israeli shekel. The US dollar, which had softened to roughly 3.02 shekels on election day, climbed rapidly to around 3.13 shekels once the final tallies were published. In parallel, the euro strengthened significantly, rising to approximately 3.47 shekels.

Market observers predict that volatility across both currency trading and the equity exchange will persist as political developments unfold. Financial analysts noted that a stronger greenback could quickly generate negative ramifications for domestic importers and drive up retail fuel prices for consumers. At the same time, lending specialists sought to reassure prospective mortgage borrowers, emphasizing that rapid exchange rate shifts should not lead them to expect immediate or automatic changes to mortgage interest rates.

Compounding market anxieties, a separate macroeconomic controversy erupted over proposals regarding international banking vulnerabilities. More than one hundred prominent economists, business executives, and former senior civil servants released a sharply worded public letter opposing a concept raised by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The prime minister had suggested that digital assets and cryptocurrencies could potentially serve as a contingency mechanism if international sanctions were ever imposed on the Israeli banking system. The signatories warned that banking sanctions would severely disrupt nearly every facet of Israel's global economic activity, paralyzing regular credit card usage, cross-border wire transfers, foreign investments, export operations, and everyday online purchases on international commerce platforms such as Amazon and AliExpress.

The signatories to the petition included Israel Prize laureate Professor Joel Mokyr, former Bank of Israel Governor Professor Jacob Frenkel, and four former directors-general of the Ministry of Finance. These distinguished experts argued that cryptocurrency cannot realistically substitute for a fully functioning international banking network. Consequently, they urged national decision-makers to focus their efforts entirely on preventing sanctions from materializing, rather than devising speculative arrangements to circumvent them. The Bank of Israel likewise criticized the idea, while Netanyahu clarified that cryptocurrencies represented merely one possibility under examination.

facts.fact: The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange fell sharply following the release of election results, reversing gains recorded on the eve of the vote.
The TA-90 index dropped by 4.6%, the TA-125 declined by 2.4%, and the TA-35 fell by 1.8%.
Construction shares fell 8.7%, real estate dropped 6.3%, and banking and insurance indices fell by approximately 5%.
The shekel weakened as the US dollar rose from roughly 3.02 shekels on election day to around 3.13 shekels, and the euro rose to about 3.47 shekels.
Market participants expect continued volatility, warning that a stronger dollar may impact importers and fuel prices, though mortgage borrowers should not expect immediate interest rate shifts.
Over 100 economists and executives published a letter criticizing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's idea to rely on cryptocurrencies if banking sanctions are imposed on Israel.
Letter signatories included Israel Prize laureate Joel Mokyr, former Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel, and four former Finance Ministry directors-general.
The Bank of Israel criticized the cryptocurrency idea, while Netanyahu stated it was merely one option under review.
